item.title: The hoop2vec bracket
item.description:
The 2027 NCAA tournament will have 76 teams, up from 68. That means a 12-game Opening Round before the usual first round of 64. hoop2vec already has a projected bracket for it, with each team’s odds of reaching each round.

The projected field

Until Selection Sunday, the field is a projection. Each conference’s automatic bid goes to its tournament champion, or to its highest-rated team until that tournament is played. At-large bids and seeds follow Power, the site’s team rating. After Selection Sunday, the real bracket replaces the projection automatically.

Exact odds

Most bracket models simulate the tournament thousands of times and count how often each team wins. hoop2vec works out the odds exactly. It has a win probability for every possible game, including each team’s travel to that game’s site. From there it can calculate each team’s chances round by round, with no simulation noise.

Right now Illinois has a 21 percent chance to win the title. That’s the best of any team, and it still means Illinois loses somewhere along the way about four times out of five. Houston is second at 14 percent, and Connecticut is the only other team above 10 percent.

Picks

The page also fills out a bracket two ways. Most likely takes the favorite in every game. Pool-optimal is built for a pool that scores rounds 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 points. It picks the likeliest champion first, then works backward to the likeliest team to reach each game given that pick. Right now the two brackets are close, and both expect about 88 points out of a possible 192.

Winning a pool takes more than being right. You also want to be right when other people in the pool are wrong. hoop2vec doesn’t know what your coworkers are picking, so it can’t help with that part.

March is also just hard to predict. In 936 past tournament games, every reasonable model I tested landed within noise of the others, including a plain efficiency rating. A whole tournament is only 75 games.

item.title: hoop2vec prospects: the draft and what comes after
item.description:
Quentin Coleman is an 18-year-old freshman guard at Illinois. He’s averaging 20.7 points a game. hoop2vec has him first on its projected board for the 2027 NBA draft, with a 65 percent chance of going in the first round.

Two models

The Prospects tab runs two models on every D-I player. The draft model estimates the chance a player is picked in the top 5, the top 14 (the lottery), the first round, and at all. It learned from every D-I player-season since 2008 and who actually got drafted.

The success model estimates the chance a player gets 8 or more Win Shares in his first four NBA seasons. Win Shares is a stat that splits a team’s wins among its players. Eight over four years is about what a steady rotation player gets. Players who went undrafted or never reached the NBA are in the data too, as misses.

Both models use the same inputs: age, height, class, recruiting ranking, team and conference strength, role, and about 30 stats adjusted for opponents. Age matters more than anything else. A freshman putting up good numbers at 18 is a much better bet than a senior putting up the same numbers at 23.

How well it works

I tested both models one draft at a time, training each only on earlier drafts. From 2012 through 2026, an average of 20 of the model’s top 30 players were drafted. A simple baseline using recruiting ranking, box plus/minus, and age got about 15.

The NBA is better at this than I am. For players who were drafted, where they were picked predicts their NBA careers better than my success model does. Teams get workouts, medical reports, and interviews. I get box scores. Adding my model to the draft slot didn’t improve on the slot alone.

It also only covers college players. International and G League prospects aren’t in it, so the board’s slots run ahead of where players will really go.

Comps

Each prospect also gets comps. A separate model learns how college stats turn into NBA stats over a player’s first four seasons. Then it finds past college players at the same stage whose projected NBA profile is closest, and shows what they became. Coleman’s closest comps include V.J. Edgecombe, Jeremiah Fears, and Dylan Harper, three freshman guards picked in the top seven in 2025.

Some things carry over to the NBA better than others. Rebounding, blocks, assists, and how many threes a player takes translate well. Shooting efficiency and overall impact translate much less.

The page also has a table of what happened by draft slot. Of college players picked in the top five from 2009 to 2022, 72 percent reached 8 Win Shares in four seasons. For second-round picks, it was 14 percent.

item.title: hoop2vec identities: how teams play
item.description:
Houston forces a turnover on about one in five possessions. It takes a lot of mid-range jumpers, rebounds 40 percent of its own misses, and sends opponents to the line often. On hoop2vec, that adds up to a Mid-Range Shot-Makers offense, a Full-Court Chaos defense, and a Deep Platoon roster.

Every team gets an identity card like this one. It describes how the team plays, separately from how good it is. The Styles tab has the full list of dimensions and archetypes and which teams fit each one.

How it’s built

It starts from play-by-play data, which logs every shot, rebound, turnover, foul, and substitution. From that I compute about 32 rates for each team. They include how often it shoots in transition, where its shots come from, how many of its baskets are assisted, and how often it ends up shooting late in the shot clock. Each rate is adjusted for opponents and home court. When there isn’t much data yet, it gets pulled toward average.

Then I take team strength out. Good teams make more shots and turn it over less, and I didn’t want a style score that was just a quality score under another name.

What’s left goes through factor analysis, which finds groups of rates that tend to move together. Transition shots, pushing the ball after defensive rebounds, and short possessions all rise and fall together, so they become one dimension called Pace & Transition. There are six of these dimensions for offense, seven for defense, and five for the roster.

Teams also get archetypes, which are clusters of teams with similar profiles. A team can sit between two. Houston is a 64 percent match for Full-Court Chaos and a 20 percent match for Conservative Pack-Line.

The cards

Each card lists strengths, vulnerabilities, and matchup notes, with the numbers behind them. Houston’s card lists Run-and-Gun Bombers as both a favorable matchup and a risky one. Its defense takes away transition chances, which those teams want. It also allows a lot of threes, which they also want.

It’s early, so most cards say low confidence. Until teams have played more games, the cards lean partly on last season.

What it doesn’t do

Style barely helps predict games. In testing, adding these style dimensions to the game forecasts improved their log loss by about 0.001 over all games. That’s tiny even for log loss, where good models are often separated by a few thousandths. In March the improvement was zero. Almost everything a matchup tells you is already in how good the two teams are.

So the forecasts leave the identities out. The Styles tab describes teams, and the ratings pick winners.

item.title: hoop2vec players: value and impact
item.description:
Thomas Haugh is a 6-foot-9 senior forward at Florida. He’s averaging 17.6 points a game and making 51 percent of his threes. On hoop2vec, he’s the most important player in the country right now.

Two numbers

Every D-I player gets two numbers. The first is Value. It’s how many points per 100 possessions better his team is with him on the floor than it would be with an average D-I player. Haugh’s is +11.1, third in the country. Vanderbilt’s Tyler Tanner, a 6-foot junior guard, is first at +11.2.

The second is Impact, which adds playing time. It’s what a player adds to his team’s rating compared with a replacement-level player, the kind of guy any team could find at the end of its bench. A great player who plays 15 minutes a game doesn’t add as much as a very good one who plays 35. Haugh plays 33 minutes a game, which makes his Impact of +10.8 the highest in D-I.

Where value comes from

Value starts from box plus/minus, a standard way to estimate a player’s contribution from his box score. hoop2vec adjusts each game for the strength of his team and the opponent, using the ratings from the morning of that game.

Early in the season there isn’t much to go on. So the number starts from a prior: what the player did last season, the typical jump for his class, and his recruiting ranking. As minutes pile up, this season’s games take over. A freshman with five good games will still be partly rated on his recruiting ranking. By February, he won’t be.

Injuries

Players also feed the game forecasts through injuries. Every morning hoop2vec reads public injury reports and gives each player an availability. A healthy player is at 100 percent, a questionable one is at 50 percent, and a player ruled out is at zero.

The team ratings already reflect the players who’ve been playing. So the adjustment only counts the difference between who’s available now and who usually plays. If a starter has missed the last three games, the ratings already know that. If he’s out tonight for the first time, the forecast moves.

Florida is a good example. Boogie Fland was playing about 25 minutes a game before a shoulder injury. With him listed as out, the model takes about two points off Florida’s rating until he’s back.

The page shows rotation players by default, which means 15 or more minutes a game. There’s a setting to show all 4,869.

item.title: The hoop2vec model that was too good
item.description:
When you test a basketball model on past seasons, you pretend it’s the morning of each game and ask what the model would have said. The hard part is making sure it only knows what someone could have known that morning. If anything from later sneaks in, the model looks better than it is. This is called leakage, and it’s easy to cause without noticing.

An early version of hoop2vec had a leak. In testing, it beat the betting lines on NCAA tournament games. A model built on free public data shouldn’t be able to do that. Sportsbooks have all the same data and a lot more reason to get it right. So I went looking for what the model knew that it shouldn’t.

Where it was

The leak was in a player stat. The stat gives every player a rating for every game, an estimate of how much he helped his team that night. To make those ratings fair, it adjusts for how good his team and the opponent are. It does that using each team’s rating from the end of the season.

That’s fine for looking back on a season, which is what the stat is meant for. It’s a problem for predicting one. Add up a team’s player ratings in November and you get a number that partly knows how good the team will be in March.

The effect was large. On its own, that one number beat the betting line in every season I checked, ten out of ten. Nothing that simple should beat a sportsbook even once.

The fix

The fix was to redo the player ratings using only what was known before each game. hoop2vec now adjusts each player’s game against the team ratings from that morning instead of the ones from the end of the season. After the change, the same number lost to the betting line in all ten seasons.

The full model got worse too. Its tournament forecasts went from beating the betting lines to trailing them slightly. That’s where an honest public-data model should be.

When a model built on public data beats the market now, I check it for leaks before I check anything else.

item.title: hoop2vec predictions: every game, every morning
item.description:
Duke plays at Florida on December 1. hoop2vec has Florida winning 78 to 73 and gives Florida a 68 percent chance. Every Division I game gets a forecast like that: a predicted score, a margin, and a win probability. They’re on the Games page and on each team’s page, and they update every morning.

On a neutral floor, the same game is close to a coin flip. Florida’s chance drops to 55 percent and the predicted margin shrinks from five points to about one. Home court is worth a few points in college basketball, and the model counts travel and rest too.

The Matchup Lab lets you set up any game this way. You pick two teams and a site. The full model runs in your browser and shows the forecast, plus how much each piece contributed: team strength, site and travel, injuries, and matchup effects.

Two models

The forecast comes from two models. The first is a neural network. It takes about 40 numbers for each team and learns how they combine. They include both ratings, shooting, rebounding, turnovers, roster strength, injuries, rest, and travel. It sees both teams at once, so it can learn that some styles match up better against others.

The second is a plain linear model. It uses team ratings, home court, travel distance, rest, and injuries, each with a fixed weight. It can’t learn matchups, but it’s harder to fool. The final forecast is 70 percent network and 30 percent linear. I picked that split by testing a range of weights on past seasons and keeping the one that did best.

Some games are harder to call than others, and the model estimates that game by game. The ±11.7 in the screenshot is that estimate for Duke and Florida. The final margin should land within about 12 points of the prediction two times out of three.

How it’s tested

To test it, I had the model predict every D-I game from 2012 through 2026 as if it were the morning of the game. For each season it could only learn from earlier seasons. It only saw injury news that was public before tip-off. That’s about 82,000 games.

The score I care about most is log loss. It punishes a forecast for being confident and wrong much more than for being unsure and wrong, and lower is better. On that measure the blend beat both of its parts and each of the ratings it’s built on. It also picked the winner in 73.5 percent of games.

The fairest comparison is a sportsbook. Last season ESPN carried DraftKings lines for about 5,500 games. The lines did a little better than the model, with a log loss of 0.542 against 0.547. This season, through 979 games, the line is still a bit ahead.

I’d be suspicious of any model built on public data that beat a sportsbook by much. Sportsbooks see the same public data I do, plus a lot of money telling them when they’re wrong.

item.title: hoop2vec ratings: one number for every team
item.description:
Illinois is the best team in college basketball right now, by about five points. That’s according to hoop2vec, which gives every Division I team a number called Power. Illinois is at +42.0. Houston is next at +37.2, and Arkansas Pine Bluff is last at −33.4.

What the number means

Power is how many points per 100 possessions a team would beat an average D-I team by on a neutral floor. A possession is one trip down the court that ends when the other team gets the ball. A typical game has about 70 of them for each team. So +42 means Illinois would beat an average team by about 29 points in a normal game. Zero is average.

Counting per 100 possessions takes pace out of it. A fast team that wins 90 to 70 and a slow team that wins 60 to 40 both won by 20. The slow team did it with fewer chances, so it was the more dominant team per trip.

The team pages put Power in more familiar terms too. Illinois would beat an average D-I team 96 percent of the time on a neutral floor. Against a typical top-25 team, it would win 71 percent of the time.

Where it comes from

There are three ratings underneath Power. The first is adjusted efficiency: points scored and allowed per 100 possessions, adjusted for who you played and where. It’s recalculated from scratch every day, and recent games count a little more. Illinois scores 131.5 points per 100 possessions against an average defense, which is the best in the country.

The second is a dynamic rating. It updates after every game and keeps track of how sure it is. Early in the season it leans on last year’s team and how much of the roster came back. The third is Elo, the system chess uses, which mostly cares about who won. It’s there as a baseline.

Those three ratings feed the game model, the same one that makes the game forecasts. So do player data, injuries, and a bunch of box score stats. To get Power, I ask that model how each team would do on a neutral floor against each of the top 100 teams. Then I shift the scale so an average team lands at zero.

The top-100 part is deliberate. Beating the 350th-best team by 40 doesn’t tell you much about how a team will do in March. Measuring everyone against good opponents keeps a team from padding its number on bad ones.

Schedule

The ratings page also lists strength of schedule. It’s the average Power of the teams you’ve played, so zero means an average D-I schedule. Florida is 6-1 against a schedule that ranks 12th. UCLA is 6-0 against one that ranks 315th. The ratings adjust for both, which is part of why Florida is fifth and UCLA is ninth.

It’s still November, and most teams have played four to seven games. The dynamic rating reports its own uncertainty, and right now Illinois’s is about plus or minus five points. That’s about the gap between first and second.

item.title: Introducing hoop2vec
item.description:
hoop2vec is a men’s college basketball site I built this fall. It rates all 365 Division I teams, forecasts every game, and updates itself every morning during the season. Everything on it comes from free public data, and it’s free to use.

The site has eight tabs. Ratings ranks every team, and Players does the same for about 4,900 players. Prospects estimates who’ll get drafted into the NBA and who’ll last once they’re there. Bracket projects the 2027 NCAA tournament and gives each team’s odds of reaching each round. Games has forecasts for upcoming games, and Matchup Lab lets you set up any game yourself. Styles describes how each team plays, and Method explains how it all works.

The name is a nod to word2vec, a method that learns a list of numbers for each word based on the words that show up around it. I liked the idea of doing that for teams and players. hoop2vec doesn’t actually use word2vec or anything like it, at least not yet. I kept the name anyway.

How it got built

I’ve been doing some version of this for a long time. About ten years ago I put a college basketball dataset on data.world. Since then I’ve built a handful of rating models and used them to fill out my own brackets. None of them made it past my laptop.

From about 2014 to 2020 I made a lot of things and shared most of them, mostly on Twitter. Some were academic and some were just for fun. Then came COVID, my first kid, and a career change. There are two kids at home now, and side projects pretty much stopped.

What changed is that I can do this kind of work from my phone. I describe what I want to Claude Code, it writes the code, and I read it and push back. Most of hoop2vec was built that way, a few minutes at a time.

hoop2vec started as two separate projects. For the first, I described what I wanted and how I thought it should work, then gave Claude Code license to build it and propose improvements. The second I directed much more closely, trying the things I thought would work and keeping what did. Then I merged the good ideas from both. Where the two overlapped, I kept whichever piece tested better, and in a few places I combined them.

I don’t love working this way. I like control, and I like knowing how every piece works down to the details. I have less of that here than I’d want. But I’ve spent a lot of years learning what makes an analysis good or bad, and this lets me put that to use much faster than I could by typing it all myself. Without it, I’d have one more rating model on my laptop.

Over the next couple of weeks I’ll write a short post about each part of the site. The first one covers the ratings.
